advisory: A finding aid for the shape of the rite, and never a book to celebrate from. Most of this Order of Mass is missing here, and every element says which of its two texts is missing and why, because they are not missing for one reason. The English side has six reasons. Twenty-five elements record a rights absence rather than text on this distribution surface. Sixteen modelled elements have official exemplars registered but no tracked payload this generator may join to them. Six variable texts belong to the Propers rather than this frame. Three elements have no fixed words, three span parts with different availability, and six are prayers the Priest says quietly for which no exact exemplar is held. The Latin side has six reasons, and they run from the reform's own new matter, which is the Holy See's and is withheld, to a rubric that has no words in any book. Where a text is missing what stands in its place is the element's received Latin incipit, which is a reference and not the prayer. THE LATIN THAT IS HERE IS NOT THIS MISSAL'S. Twenty elements carry Latin, and at every one of them it is the facing column of an 1861 Philadelphia lay hand missal printing the ancient prayer this Order of Mass received. The controlling 2008 Latin is not distributable on this surface and is not served as an element text anywhere on this page. Each of the twenty says beside its own words which prayer of that older book it is, at which printed page and leaf, which accidents of that printing it carries unnormalised, and whether its identity with the controlling edition has been established by a collation this repository holds or is so far only asserted. Five are established; fifteen are not, and they say so.
derived_from: The order, the numbering, the Latin incipits, the speakers and the conditions are transcribed from this repository's own collated study of the Order of Mass, src/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/postconciliar/2008-latin-2011-us-english/ordinary/00-order-of-mass, and in particular its research/sequence-inventory.md, which gives one row per received boundary in the Missal's own order and numbering against the 2008 editio typica tertia emendata. That study's own scope record states the boundary this file inherits: the Latin is quoted there where an argument requires it, as evidence and not as text for recitation, and the approved English is not reproduced. The Latin texts here are drawn from a DIFFERENT BOOK, and that is the whole of what has to be understood about them: the six ordinarium, praefationes and canon-missae `-la` artifacts of edition.eugene-cummiskey.roman-missal-english-laity.philadelphia-1861, which transcribe the facing Latin column of an 1861 Philadelphia lay hand missal from a registered scan at 640 dpi, one physical line per printed block, each row carrying its own printed page, Internet Archive leaf and transcriber's note. Those artifacts are already the Latin of this project's 1962 frame; here they are joined to a second calendar, element by element, because the older book prints the ancient prayer the postconciliar Missal received and for no other reason. Nothing is transcribed afresh for this file and nothing is normalised: the join names artifact rows that already exist and already carry their hash.

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Gloria in excelsis, printed page xix, Internet Archive leaf 29, the hymn complete in one block. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008. The repository holds and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list, but the controlling 2008 text is not distributable on this surface and is not served here; these are the 1861 printing's words. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book opens with a two-line drop G followed by LORIA in capitals, given here as GLORIA; it reads bonae voluntatis and Rex coelestis with the ae- and oe-ligatures, Jesu Christe with a J twice, and sets the closing Amen in italic. COLLATED, and on a finding rather than on a comparison of two strings, which is a weaker footing than the three elements that carry both. The cited study's endnote to n. 8 states in terms that the Latin text at n. 8 is unchanged from the older Roman form, and the study's own account of its method states that both books were read directly for that comparison. It quotes no 2002 Latin at this element, so no word-level comparison could be made here and none is claimed.
translations.text: GLORIA in excelsis Deo, et in terra pax hominibus bonæ voluntatis. Laudamus te; benedicimus te; adoramus te; glorificamus te. Gratias agimus tibi propter magnam gloriam tuam, Domine Deus, Rex cœlestis, Deus Pater omnipotens. Domine Fili unigenite Jesu Christe. Domine Deus, Agnus Dei, Filius Patris, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. Qui tollis peccata mundi, suscipe deprecationem nostram. Qui sedes ad dexteram Patris, miserere nobis. Quoniam tu solus sanctus. Tu solus Dominus. Tu solus altissimus, Jesu Christe, cum Sancto Spiritu, in gloria Dei Patris. Amen.

elements.name: The Nicene Creed
elements.note: Said on Sundays and solemnities, with a bow prescribed at et homo factus est.
elements.speaker: all

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Credo, printed pages xxi-xxii, Internet Archive leaves 31-32, joined from that book's own three blocks. The Latin of the Missale Romanum, editio typica tertia 2002 with its emended reprint of 2008 is not served here. The repository holds and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list, but that evidence does not establish this word identity; these are the 1861 printing's words. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: a two-line drop C followed by REDO in capitals, given here as CREDO; the ae- and oe-ligatures at terrae, coeli, coelis, saecula, saeculi; Jesum Christum and judicare with a J; ET HOMO FACTUS EST set in full capitals with the book's own asterisk keying a footnote at the foot of xxii; and Et EXPECTO, not exspecto, the word standing whole and unbroken on its own line. The second block runs over the page break, breaking at ex Maria Vir- / gine, and heavy inking at the head of xxii fills the s and e of sepultus, which the transcriber read from the surviving strokes and did not repair from any other book. The printing carries the Filioque, qui ex Patre Filioque procedit. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass treats n. 18 at 00-order-of-mass/sections/30-creed-and-universal-prayer.tex:16-24 and names the Nicene Creed among the texts retained with little or no change of wording at :90-synthesis.tex:47-55, on a comparison for which it states that both books were read directly. It quotes no 2002 Latin of the symbol, so no word-level comparison has been made. The two Latin texts are conventionally taken to be identical and that convention has not been checked here.
translations.text:
CREDO in unum Deum Patrem omnipotentem, factorem cœli et terræ, visibilium omnium et invisibilium.
Et in unum Dominum Jesum Christum, Filium Dei unigenitum, et ex Patre natum ante omnia sæcula. Deum de Deo: Lumen de Lumine; Deum verum de Deo vero; genitum non factum; consubstantialem Patri, per quem omnia facta sunt. Qui propter nos homines, et propter nostram salutem descendit de cœlis. Et incarnatus est de Spiritu Sancto, ex Maria Virgine: ET HOMO FACTUS EST*. Crucifixus etiam pro nobis sub Pontio Pilato, passus et sepultus est. Et resurrexit tertia die secundum Scripturas. Et ascendit in cœlum, sedet ad dexteram Patris. Et iterum venturus est cum gloria judicare vivos et mortuos; cujus regni non erit finis.
Et in Spiritum Sanctum, Dominum et vivificantem, qui ex Patre Filioque procedit: qui cum Patre et Filio simul adoratur, et conglorificatur; qui locutus est per prophetas. Et unam sanctam Catholicam et Apostolicam Ecclesiam. Confiteor unum Baptisma in remissionem peccatorum. Et expecto resurrectionem mortuorum, et vitam venturi sæculi. Amen.

THE WITNESS MISPRINTS nodie FOR hodie, and it is carried as printed and not corrected: the letter is an n, with no ascender, read at 200 per cent magnification against the h of hoc on the same page and recorded in the artifact's own transcriber's note. It is that printer's error. Nothing here attributes it to the Missal, and correcting it silently would have manufactured a target witness this project has not established. The visually checked 1862 Pustet page at passage.catholic-church.missale-romanum.pustet-ratisbon-1862.ordo-missae-leaf-303 prints hodie and confirms only that the 1861 n is not the older prayer's general reading; it does not establish the postconciliar target. This repository's study of this Order of Mass states at n. 26, in 00-order-of-mass/sections/40-preparation-of-the-gifts.tex:108-110, that the prayer is taken from the Song of the Three Young Men and is retained from the older Order, and it quotes the 2002 Latin of the opening clause only, as far as suscipiamur a te, Domine. translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Orate fratres and Suscipiat Dominus, printed page xxvii, Internet Archive leaf 37, joined from the book's own two blocks. The controlling 2008 text is not distributable on this surface and is not served here. The repository holds and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list; the words carried here are the 1861 printing's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: Fratres is capitalised and patrem is not, as the book sets them; the Latin column points a comma after nominis sui where its own facing English points none; there is a comma after nostram; Ecclesiae suae sanctae carries the ae-ligature throughout; and the response's R. mark is the book's, which prefixes the answer in both columns and prefixes the summons in neither. COLLATED. The cited study quotes the 2002 Latin of both texts at n. 29 and its endnote states that both are retained from the older Roman Order without material change; setting that quotation beside these two rows, they agree word for word, the only differences being the capitalisation, the pointing and the ligatures named above.

It misprints ereas for creas—the e was verified at 250 percent—and prints no cross signs over the three verbs; the error is retained and attributed only to that source. The target study quotes no complete n. 97 Latin, so this is an uncollated antecedent and no target identity is claimed.
translations.text: Per quem hæc omnia, Domine, semper bona ereas, sanctificas, vivificas, benedicis, et præstas nobis.

elements.latin_incipit: Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso
elements.name: The final doxology
elements.note: The people's Amen closes it. Here per omnia saecula saeculorum is part of the doxology itself; in the 1962 book it follows as a separate versicle of priest and minister.
elements.speaker: priest

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Per ipsum and the versicle that closes its Canon, printed pages xxxviii-xxxix, Internet Archive leaves 48-49, joined from that book's own two blocks. The controlling 2008 text is not distributable on this surface and is not served here. The repository holds and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list, but that evidence does not establish this word identity; these are the 1861 printing's words. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book prints no cross signs in this block, which the older Roman rite marks five times; it reads saecula saeculorum with the ae-ligature, set unbroken here where the same versicle at the foot of xxvii prints a full stop after saecula; and it sets the Amen in italic. THE SHAPE DIFFERS AND THE MARKS SHOW IT: the witness's P. and R. divide the closing versicle between priest and minister, which is the older Order, where this Missal makes per omnia saecula saeculorum the end of the doxology itself and the people's Amen answers the whole. The marks are the witness's and are not this Missal's rubric. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass records at 00-order-of-mass/sections/55-roman-canon.tex:114 that the prayer text is substantially identical from Te igitur to Per ipsum apart from the changes to the dominical words, which fall elsewhere in the Canon and not in this element. It quotes no 2002 Latin of the doxology, so no word-level comparison has been made.
translations.text:
Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso, est tibi Deo Patri omnipotenti, in unitate Spiritus Sancti, omnis honor et gloria.
P. Per omnia sæcula sæculorum. R. Amen.

elements.name: The Lord's Prayer
elements.note: The Roman Rite does not say the prayer continuously: the doxology follows the embolism Libera nos rather than preceding it.
elements.speaker: all

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Praeceptis salutaribus and Pater noster, printed page xxxix, Internet Archive leaf 49, joined from that book's own two blocks. The controlling 2008 text is not distributable on this surface and is not served here. The repository holds and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list, but that evidence does not establish this word identity; these are the 1861 printing's words. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the invitation opens with a two-line drop P followed by Raeceptis, a capital R and the rest lower-case, with the ae-ligature, given here as printed; the prayer reads coelis and coelo with the oe-ligature and quotidianum for cotidianum; and the book runs the response R. Sed libera nos a malo and the priest's italic P. Amen. into the same block, which is the older Order's division of the prayer between priest and ministers and not this Missal's. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass quotes the 2002 Latin of the INVITATION at n. 124, in 00-order-of-mass/sections/70-communion-rite.tex:19-23, and that quotation and this witness's first row agree word for word. It quotes no 2002 Latin of the Our Father itself, which is the larger half of this element and has been compared with nothing. The study names the Pater noster with its introduction among the texts retained with little or no change of wording, and records the change that is real: the people now say it with the priest, where in the older Roman Order the priest said it and the ministers answered the last petition.
translations.text:
PRæceptis salutaribus moniti, et divina institutione formati, audemus dicere:
Pater noster, qui es in cœlis, sanctificetur nomen tuum: adveniat regnum tuum: fiat voluntas tua sicut in cœlo, et in terra: panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie; et dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris: et ne nos inducas in tentationem: R. Sed libera nos a malo. P. Amen.

elements.latin_incipit: Libera nos, quaesumus, Domine, ab omnibus malis
elements.name: The embolism
elements.speaker: priest

elements.latin_incipit: Domine Iesu Christe, qui dixisti Apostolis tuis
elements.name: The prayer for peace
elements.speaker: priest

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at printed page xl, Internet Archive leaf 50. It prints the versicle and response as one source-owned block without crosses. The independently registered 1862 Pustet page image at passage.catholic-church.missale-romanum.pustet-ratisbon-1862.ordo-missae-leaf-347 corroborates the older wording and prints three crosses in the chanted versicle. Nothing is normalised between the two witnesses. UNCOLLATED: the postconciliar study quotes Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum at n. 127, matching the versicle word for word, but it does not establish Et cum spiritu tuo at this number. The response is attested elsewhere in the target book and that is not a collation of this element. The older source block is therefore carried as an honestly labelled antecedent, never as the target text, and no complete identity is claimed.
translations.text: P. Pax Domini sit semper vobiscum. R. Et cum spiritu tuo.

elements.name: The invitation and exchange of peace
elements.note: Expressly conditional, pro opportunitate. The older witnesses instead print the distinct clerical pax Pax tecum; their words are not this invitation.
elements.speaker: all

elements.latin_incipit: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi
elements.name: Agnus Dei
elements.note: Repeatable as long as the fraction lasts.
elements.speaker: all

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Agnus Dei, printed page xl, Internet Archive leaf 50. The controlling 2008 text is not distributable on this surface and is not served here. The repository holds and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list, but that evidence does not establish this word identity; these are the 1861 printing's words. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book does not write the invocation out three times. It sets three asterisks at the head of three short lines, * miserere nobis, twice and then * dona nobis pacem., the asterisk marking where Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi is resumed, and they are run in here as the sibling English row runs them. A reader must expand them as the book intends and not read four clauses where the rite has three invocations. UNCOLLATED: the identity of this text with the controlling edition's is not established here. This repository's study of this Order of Mass describes n. 130 at 00-order-of-mass/sections/70-communion-rite.tex:86-91 and names the Agnus Dei among the texts retained with little or no change of wording, on a comparison for which it states that both books were read directly; it quotes the 2002 Latin of the ending dona nobis pacem only, which this witness matches. The invocation itself has been compared with nothing.
translations.text: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, * miserere nobis, * miserere nobis, * dona nobis pacem.

elements.latin_incipit: Domine Iesu Christe, Fili Dei vivi
elements.name: The priest's private preparation
elements.note: Two forms; the priest chooses one and says it inaudibly.

elements.note: The people answer Domine, non sum dignus, once, with the priest.
elements.speaker: all

translations.note: ANTECEDENT, NOT THE CONTROLLING EDITION. The Latin here is the facing column of the 1861 Philadelphia Cummiskey hand missal at its Quod ore sumpsimus, printed pages xlii-xliii, Internet Archive leaves 52-53, the block running over the page break at fiat nobis re- / medium. The controlling 2008 text is not distributable on this surface and is not served here. The repository holds and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list; the words carried here are the 1861 printing's. Carried as printed and normalised nowhere: the book points a comma after temporali which the study's quotation of the 2002 text does not. COLLATED. The cited study quotes the 2002 Latin of this prayer entire at n. 137 and calls it a post-Communion prayer of great antiquity, retained; set beside this row the two agree word for word, the sole divergence being that comma.
translations.text: Quod ore sumpsimus, Domine, pura mente capiamus, et de munere temporali, fiat nobis remedium sempiternum.

elements.note: A simple blessing; or a solemn blessing or prayer over the people, introduced by Inclinate vos ad benedictionem; or, for a bishop, the pontifical form with Sit nomen Domini benedictum and Adiutorium nostrum.

slots_derived_from: Where each proper of the day stands inside this frame is read from the same collated study as the order of the elements, and each slot's locus is the Missal's own numbering of the element it is anchored to. This repository holds and has read a verified witness of the 2002 Ordo Missae and the official bounded list of the 2008 variations, but no complete facsimile of the controlling 2008 reprint. Unlike the 1962 frame, these placements therefore rest on that study and on the Missal's numbering rather than on a complete 2008 exemplar; every slot below anchors to an element whose number this file already carries.
title: The Order of Mass

translations.caution: NOT the Latin of the Missale Romanum. The controlling 2008 Latin is a work of the Holy See, is under copyright, is not distributable on this surface, and is not served under this witness; no element here claims that the 1861 words are that book's text. The repository does hold and has read a verified 2002 Ordo witness and the official bounded 2008 variation list, but that evidence does not establish every antecedent identity. What is here is the facing Latin column of an 1861 Philadelphia lay hand missal - never an altar book, never an approved liturgical translation, and pre-1955 in its rubrics and its discipline - which prints the ancient prayers this Order of Mass received. It is joined element by element, and only where an element's Latin is that ancient prayer; where the reform composed, recast or rearranged, nothing is carried and the element says why. Its orthography and its misprints are its own and are carried as printed: justum for iustum, Jesu for Iesu, Et expecto for Et exspecto, the ae- and oe-ligatures, and nodie for hodie at In spiritu humilitatis are the 1861 printer's and not the Holy See's. Every element carrying Latin states beside its own words which prayer of that book it is, at which printed page and Internet Archive leaf, which accidents it carries, and whether its identity with the controlling edition has been established or is so far only asserted. Nothing here may be used for recitation.
translations.label: Antecedent Latin (NOT the Missale Romanum's text): the facing Latin column of The Roman Missal translated into the English language for the use of the laity, first revised edition (Philadelphia: Eugene Cummiskey, 1861)

variants.name: Penitential Act
variants.what: The Missal prints three forms at Ordo Missae nn. 4-6, and one form is used in this place. The source study records the three forms and their shared bounds at src/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/postconciliar/2008-latin-2011-us-english/ordinary/00-order-of-mass/sections/10-introductory-rites.tex:88-105. The first is marked as the display default only because it is the first form the Missal prints; that is not a preference or an appointment for a day.

variants.name: Creed
variants.what: The Missal prints the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed at n. 18 and permits the Apostles' Creed at n. 19 in its place, especially in Lent and Eastertide, as recorded and sourced in src/claude/liturgy/roman-rite/postconciliar/2008-latin-2011-us-english/ordinary/00-order-of-mass/sections/30-creed-and-universal-prayer.tex:16-24. The Nicene Creed is marked as the display default because it is the principal form printed first; the marker does not appoint a Creed on a day when none is said.

variants.name: Eucharistic Prayer
variants.what: The postconciliar Missal prints four Eucharistic Prayers and the priest chooses among them; the first may always be used, and the Missal states where the fourth may not. The 1962 Missal has one Canon and no such choice, so this control belongs to this missal alone. The option marked default here is the first the Missal itself prints. That is the only order this project can state without preferring one prayer over another, and it is not a recommendation.
